## Ideas about work and democracy in the Progressive Era United States

I am interested in how intellectuals expressed ideas about work and democracy in
what some historians call the Progressive Era. I am especially interested in how
these ideas shaped some of the political reform movements that took root in the
same period, and in how we should understand the people who constituted the
ideology of reformism that we could call "Progressivism."

I wrote a series of articles on some of the ideology's major exponents and
expanded it into a book, *A Working Democracy: Progressivism and the Politics of
Work*, adding two more chapters (on W.E.B. Du Bois and Charlotte Perkins Gilman)
and an interpretive introduction and conclusion that assess and analyze the
Progressive movement as a whole. One contribution the book makes is a new
interpretation of Progressivism as an ideology that centers work, an ideology
that tried to make space for cross-class solidarity; part of that argument is
that Du Bois belongs among the Progressives, alongside Jane Addams, John Dewey,
and Gilman. It also shows how Herbert Croly of *The New Republic* magazine
helped to synthesize and popularize their ideas in the period, highlighting some
prominent themes as he did and eliding others. I conclude by
suggesting that there are aspects of the Progressives' ideology of work that are
worth keeping alive today, most of which are rooted in the Progressive
intellectuals' understanding of themselves as workers. Despite having finished
the book, my teaching and writing continue my interest in the period and its
echoes in our own day.

- *A Working Democracy: Progressivism and the Politics of Work.*
  University of Notre Dame Press, accepted for publication.
